title-group.article-title: Osimertinib-associated cardiac dysfunction in epidermal growth factor receptor-mutant non-small cell lung cancer: a single-center three-case series requiring hospitalization

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Osimertinib is frequently used for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), whereas cardiotoxicity signals, including left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) decline, heart failure (HF), and corrected QT interval prolongation, have been documented.

sec.title: Cases
sec.p: We describe three patients without clinical HF at baseline who were hospitalized for symptomatic HF with newly documented LVEF decline during osimertinib therapy. Case 1 (a 61-year-old woman with prior anthracycline exposure) developed early HF at approximately 1 to 2 months. Recovery was incomplete despite discontinuation and guideline-directed HF therapy, and she died at approximately 10 months after HF onset owing to cancer progression. Case 2 (a 72-year-old woman) presented at 12 months. Osimertinib was continued under HF therapy, and LVEF recovered. Case 3 (a 74-year-old woman; fourth-line osimertinib) presented at 60 months (ultra-late). Following a 2-month interruption and HF therapy, osimertinib was reintroduced without recurrence, and LVEF recovered.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: These cases illustrate that osimertinib-associated cardiac dysfunction can develop from early to ultra-late phases and that selective rechallenge may be considered following HF therapy optimization and recovery with close monitoring. Comparative risk or incidence was not evaluated.

list-item.p: Osimertinib cardiac dysfunction ranged from early to ultra-late onset.
Three patients were hospitalized for symptomatic HF with new LVEF decline.
HF therapy stabilized or improved cardiac function in two patients.
Selective osimertinib rechallenge was feasible with close monitoring.
Structured cardiac follow-up is advisable throughout treatment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Osimertinib, a third-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is commonly administered in patients with EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Cardiotoxicity signals, including left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) decline, heart failure (HF), and corrected QT interval (QTc) prolongation, have been documented. Baseline and on-treatment cardiac assessment is recommended [[1], [2], [3]]. Recent real-world cohorts have suggested an overall cardiotoxicity rate of approximately 5%, with advanced age, prior HF, atrial fibrillation, and low baseline global longitudinal strain (GLS) as risk factors, and recovery is frequently attainable [4]. First-line multicenter data have also indicated QTc prolongation and cardiac dysfunction occurring at more than 6 months [5]. Some comparative analyses have suggested a higher cardiac event frequency with osimertinib versus other EGFR-TKIs [6]. To illustrate the range of onset timing and management (discontinuation, continuation, and post-interruption rechallenge) and guide clinical evaluation and decision-making, we describe three hospitalized cases of symptomatic HF with new LVEF decline during osimertinib therapy.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This case series adhered to the CAse REport (CARE) guidelines. All patients provided written informed consent for publication, and the institutional ethics committee approved this study (approval number: 02-28). We identified patients at a single center who had no clinical HF at baseline, subsequently developed symptomatic HF necessitating hospitalization during osimertinib therapy, and whose clinical course could be documented. Causality was evaluated using the World Health Organization–Uppsala Monitoring Center (WHO–UMC) criteria and reported per case (Possible/Probable) [7].

sec.title: Case presentations
sec.p:
A 61-year-old woman with EGFR L858R started first-line osimertinib 80 mg. Previous medical history encompassed breast cancer treated with anthracycline-containing chemotherapy. Baseline LVEF was 64%. At approximately 1 to 2 months, she developed exertional dyspnea and edema, requiring hospitalization. Chest imaging revealed bilateral pleural effusion. LVEF was 22%, the B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) level was 1834.4 pg/mL, and QTc was 376 ms. Osimertinib was discontinued, and HF therapy (tolvaptan, furosemide, spironolactone, and bisoprolol) was initiated. Recovery was incomplete (LVEF was 29% at 8 months), and she died at approximately 10 months after HF onset owing to cancer progression. Prior anthracycline exposure could not be excluded as a contributing factor (WHO–UMC: Possible).•
Case 2

A 72-year-old woman with EGFR L858R initiated first-line osimertinib 80 mg (baseline LVEF, 62%). At 11 months (1 month before HF onset), the dose was reduced to 40 mg owing to rash. At 12 months, she presented with orthopnea, necessitating hospitalization. Bilateral pleural effusion and cardiac silhouette enlargement were observed (LVEF, 21%; BNP, 1883.5 pg/mL; and QTc, 412 ms). Osimertinib was continued with HF therapy (tolvaptan, furosemide, spironolactone, and carvedilol). LVEF improved to 37% and 60% at 11 and 19 months after HF onset, respectively. Osimertinib was later discontinued owing to tumor progression, and no subsequent LVEF worsening was observed (WHO–UMC: Possible).•
Case 3

A 74-year-old woman (EGFR exon 19 deletion, T790M-positive following gefitinib therapy) received fourth-line osimertinib 80 mg. Pretreatment LVEF was not documented. At 27 months, LVEF was 63%, which was subsequently used as the reference. At 60 months, she developed dyspnea and was hospitalized owing to bilateral pleural effusion and pulmonary edema. The following were her laboratory parameters: LVEF, 33%; BNP, 1509.9 pg/mL; and QTc, 446 ms. HF therapy (furosemide, spironolactone, and carvedilol) was initiated, and osimertinib was held for 2 months and subsequently reintroduced at the same dose following symptom improvement. She remained free from HF recurrence. At 9 months following rechallenge, her LVEF was 56% (WHO–UMC: Probable). A summary is presented in Table 1, and timelines are depicted in Fig. 1.Table 1

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p:
This series presents three hospitalized cases of symptomatic HF with new LVEF decline during osimertinib therapy. Onset timing varied, with cases occurring early at approximately 1 to 2 months, at 12 months, and at 60 months (ultra-late). Management differed across cases, including discontinuation, continuation under HF therapy, and rechallenge after treatment interruption. Standard heart failure therapy refers to treatment with diuretics, beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and other agents as appropriate, alone or in combination, as clinically indicated.

Previous reports have demonstrated osimertinib-related cardiotoxicity signals, including LVEF decline, HF, and QTc prolongation [[1], [2], [3]]. Real-world data have suggested an overall cardiotoxicity rate of approximately 5%, with advanced age, pre-existing cardiac disease, and low baseline GLS as risk factors. Notably, recovery is generally attainable [4]. First-line multicenter data have revealed that events may occur at more than 6 months [5]. Smaller series have shown early onset events with recovery following interruption [13]. Comparative analyses have suggested higher event frequencies with osimertinib than with other EGFR-TKIs, warranting vigilance. However, the present series was not designed to test comparative risk or estimate incidence [6].

Mechanistically, anticancer drug cardiotoxicity has been associated with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction [14]. EGFR/ErbB (neuregulin-1/HER2) signaling inhibition may attenuate cardioprotective pathways [15]. The dual-hit (multiple-hit) concept, combining impaired survival signaling with elevated oxidative stress, has been proposed in HER2-targeted therapy, providing a valuable interpretive framework [16]. In Case 1, the limited recovery following discontinuation suggests cumulative vulnerabilities (e.g., prior anthracycline exposure). However, causal certainty is unachievable with case-level data. Clinically, the time course, exclusion of alternative etiologies, and dechallenge/rechallenge responses should be integrated case by case.

Regarding rechallenge, previous case reports have documented successful reintroduction following recovery [9,17], and real-world experience suggests that selective rechallenge is occasionally attempted [18]. In our series, in Case 3, osimertinib was restarted without developing recurrence at follow-up. Rechallenge is not universally recommended, but may be considered following HF therapy optimization and documented recovery, with individualized monitoring (echocardiography, electrocardiography, and biomarkers as appropriate). The educational value of this series lies in exemplifying time-course heterogeneity (early to ultra-late) and pragmatic management options within a single consistent framework.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This single-center retrospective series encompasses only hospitalized symptomatic cases of HF. Asymptomatic LVEF decline and milder outpatient-managed cases were not captured. Echocardiography was performed for cardiac assessments, with some instances of lacking true pretreatment baseline data. Previous therapies and comorbidities cannot be fully excluded as contributing factors. Consequently, incidence estimation and between-drug comparisons are beyond the scope of this series, and generalizability is limited. Validating GLS-based risk stratification and long-term outcome analysis in first-line cohorts are outside the scope of our dataset.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Osimertinib-associated cardiac dysfunction can develop from early to ultra-late phases of therapy. We presented three hospitalized cases, demonstrating that onset timing and management (discontinuation, continuation, or post-interruption rechallenge) vary between patients. Following recovery and with vigilant monitoring, selective rechallenge may be considered in selected cases.
